Infamy
ĭn´fă-mĭ
n. (evil report; public disgrace — rendering Hebrew dibbah)
Latin infamia, from in- (not) and fama (report, fame) — the loss of good report. The Hebrew dibbah means slander or evil report, whether deserved or not.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Infamy is the loss of a good name, and Scripture treats it as a real and heavy loss. Solomon warns the man who spreads another's secret: “Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away” (Pro 25:10) — a disgrace that will not leave once it settles. Ezekiel uses the word of a nation stripped and mocked: the mountains of Israel are “taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people” (Eze 36:3). The Hebrew behind it means evil report, and it is the same word used of the slanderous report the ten spies brought back of the land. So infamy can be the just consequence of sin, as in Proverbs, or the unjust portion of God's people in the mouths of their enemies, as in Ezekiel — where the chapter goes on to promise that God will vindicate His own name and cleanse them. Against the whole subject Scripture sets a plain valuation: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold” (Pro 22:1), and “A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth” (Ecc 7:1). A reputation is worth guarding, and worth more than money — but not more than obedience, since Christ Himself made Himself of no reputation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines infamy as total loss of reputation; public disgrace; and also the loss of character incident to a conviction of an infamous crime.

expand to see more

IN'FAMY, n. Total loss of reputation; public disgrace.

2. Qualities which are detested and despised; qualities notoriously bad and scandalous.

3. In law, that loss of character or public disgrace which a convict incurs, and by which he is rendered incapable of being a witness.

IN'FAMOUS, a. Of ill report; having a reputation of the worst kind; branded with infamy.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 25:10 — "Lest he that heareth it put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away."

Ezekiel 36:3 — "Therefore prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because they have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that ye might be a possession unto the residue of the heathen, and ye are taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people:"

Proverbs 22:1 — "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold."

Ecclesiastes 7:1 — "A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth."

Modern Corruption

Public disgrace is inflicted as entertainment and preserved indefinitely, while the reputation Scripture calls better than riches is treated as a thing anyone may destroy at will.

expand to see more

Proverbs 25:10 warns that an infamy, once fastened, may not turn away, and it says so as a caution to the man doing the fastening. Scripture regards the destruction of another's good name as a serious injury, which is why the ninth commandment exists and why the law required two witnesses before a matter was established. The present machinery for spreading an evil report is faster and more permanent than anything Solomon imagined, and it is used casually, for amusement, and without the possibility of correction. A Christian who repeats a report he has not verified has done a thing Scripture treats as a form of theft.

The other side of the word is comfort. Ezekiel 36 finds God's own people an infamy in the lips of talkers — deserved, since their sin had brought them there — and the chapter answers not with a defence of their conduct but with the promise that God will sanctify His great name and cleanse them from all their filthiness. Vindication belongs to God and He undertakes it. This is why a believer may be commanded to entrust his reputation to God rather than to fight for it: our Lord made Himself of no reputation, was numbered with the transgressors, and is now given a name above every name.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dibbah (H1681), an evil report, slander, infamy — Proverbs 25:10, Ezekiel 36:3, Numbers 13:32; shem (H8034), name, in Proverbs 22:1.

expand to see more

Hebrew dibbah (H1681) — defaming, evil report, slander; Proverbs 25:10, Ezekiel 36:3, and Numbers 13:32 of the spies' evil report.

Hebrew shem (H8034) — name, reputation; Proverbs 22:1 and Ecclesiastes 7:1, where a good name outweighs riches and ointment.

Latin infamia — the undoing of fama, report; the word names a loss, not a quality.

Ezekiel 36 answers infamy with God vindicating His own great name, and cleansing His people.

Philippians 2:7 sets the limit on defending one's name: Christ made Himself of no reputation.

Usage

"“Thine infamy turn not away” — some disgraces do not lift."

"“Taken up in the lips of talkers” — a nation made a byword."

"“A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches” — and yet not above obedience."
